note: Prepared from the unit title and the trade's usual practice. An instructor must read and correct it, and mark it Ready, before it is opened for an intake.

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. You may use a calculator unless the instructor says otherwise. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: The area of a rectangle is A = L × W. Which form of the formula gives the width W?
Heat input (kJ/mm) = (V × I × 60) ÷ (1000 × S), where V is arc volts, I is amps and S is travel speed in mm/min. What is the heat input for a weld made at 24 V, 200 A and 300 mm/min?
Using the same heat input formula, what happens to the heat input if the travel speed is doubled and nothing else changes?
options: It doubles to twice the value
It falls to half its value

questions.stem: Pressure = force ÷ area, or P = F ÷ A. Which form gives the force F?
A plasma torch cuts 1.8 m of plate in 3 minutes. What is its cutting speed in mm/min?
A batch of 80 welds was inspected, and 6 were rejected. What is the reject rate?
A part should be 250 mm long but measures 247 mm. What is the percentage error?
Steel costs J$350 000 a tonne. A job needs 2.4 tonnes. What does the steel cost?
A supplier gives a 12.5% discount on an order of J$64 000. What is the price after the discount?
The price of a length of pipe rises from J$4 000 to J$4 600. What is the percentage increase?
A shielding gas is mixed argon to carbon dioxide in the ratio 4 : 1. What percentage of the mix is carbon dioxide?
A right-angled triangle has sides of 500 mm and 1200 mm meeting at the right angle. How long is the third side (the hypotenuse)?
A stair stringer rises 2100 mm over a level going of 2800 mm. How long is the stringer, measured along the slope?
In a right-angled triangle, which ratio gives the tangent (tan) of an angle?
A ramp must rise 500 mm at an angle of 20° to the level. How long is the ramp along its slope? (sin 20° = 0.342, tan 20° = 0.364)
A calculator shows 1462.0468 mm for a brace length. The tape measure reads to 1 mm. What should be written on the cut list?
A roof rafter is 3 m long and makes 25° with the level. How high does its top end rise above its bottom end? (sin 25° = 0.423, cos 25° = 0.906)
Why is the 3-4-5 rule used when setting out a frame?
options: It gives the right weld size for the frame
It sets the correct paint thickness
It checks that a corner is a true right angle
It gives the length of steel to order for the frame job

questions.stem: A gusset is a right-angled triangle with sides of 300 mm and 200 mm meeting at the right angle. What is its area?
A plate 1200 mm × 800 mm has a 400 mm diameter hole cut from its centre. What area of plate is left, to two decimal places? (π = 3.142)
How many square millimetres are there in 1 square metre?
The outside of a tank is to be painted: its curved side and its top only. The tank is a cylinder 1.0 m in diameter and 1.5 m high. What area is painted, to one decimal place? (π = 3.142)
A paint covers 8 m² per litre for each coat. Two coats are needed on 36 m². How much paint is needed?
A round steel bar is 25 mm in diameter and 2 m long. Taking steel as 7850 kg/m³ and π as 3.142, what is its mass?
A steel pipe has an outside diameter of 114 mm and a wall 6 mm thick. What is its inside diameter?
A rectangular tank measures 2.0 m × 1.2 m × 0.9 m inside. How many litres does it hold when full?
A square hollow section has a cross-section area of 560 mm². Taking steel as 7850 kg/m³, what is the mass of 1 m of it?
A crane is rated to lift 2 tonnes (its safe working load). The team wants to lift 12 plates, each 1.5 m × 1.5 m × 10 mm, in one lift. Can this be done? (Steel is 7850 kg/m³.)
A curved handrail follows a quarter circle with a radius of 2.0 m. How long is the rail? (π = 3.142)
A gas pipe has an inside diameter of 50 mm. What is the area of its bore, to the nearest whole number? (π = 3.142)
A cut-off wheel 355 mm in diameter turns at 3800 rev/min. What is the speed at its rim, in metres per second? (π = 3.142)
A hole is shown on a drawing as Ø20 +0.2 / −0.0 mm. Which measured size is acceptable?
A 6 mm fillet weld with equal legs has a cross-section shaped like a right-angled triangle. What is its cross-section area?
For a fillet weld with equal legs, the throat is about 0.7 × the leg length. What is the throat of an 8 mm leg fillet weld?
A fillet weld has a cross-section of 32 mm² and is 2.5 m long in total. What is the volume of weld metal?
Steel weld metal has a mass of about 7.85 g per cm³. What is the mass of 80 cm³ of weld metal?
A job needs 4.5 kg of deposited weld metal. About 60% of an electrode's mass ends up as weld metal. What mass of electrodes should be drawn from stores?
A cutting torch uses oxygen at 30 L/min. How much oxygen is used in 45 minutes of cutting?
An argon cylinder holds about 9 000 litres of gas. A TIG welder uses 10 L/min. About how many hours of welding does the cylinder give?
In an 8-hour shift, a welder's arc is burning for 2.5 hours in total. What percentage of the shift is arc time?
Five parts measure 498, 502, 500, 497 and 503 mm. What is their mean (average) length?
For the same five parts (498, 502, 500, 497 and 503 mm), what is the range?
A drawing is at a scale of 1:20. Two holes are 37 mm apart on the drawing. How far apart are they on the real part?
An old procedure asks for a preheat of 250 °F. What is this in °C? (°C = (°F − 32) × 5 ÷ 9)
Why should a calculated answer be checked with a rough estimate before steel is cut?
options: Calculators are never right with decimals
So the job takes longer and costs more
To catch a slip before steel is wasted
Because the customer likes rough figures

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences and show your working. You may use a calculator unless the instructor says otherwise. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: In a right-angled triangle, what is the name of the longest side, opposite the right angle?
A ramp is 4 m long along its slope and rises 0.6 m. What is its slope as a percentage (rise ÷ level run × 100), to one decimal place?
A pipe is 60.3 mm outside diameter and 52.5 mm inside diameter. What is the mass of a 6 m length, in kg, to one decimal place? (π = 3.142, steel 7850 kg/m³)
The steel for a job costs J$48 000, and the shop adds a 25% mark-up. What is the selling price of the steel, in J$?
What is the throat thickness, in mm, of a fillet weld with equal 10 mm legs? (Throat = 0.7 × leg.)
How many millimetres are there in 5/8 inch, to one decimal place? (1 inch = 25.4 mm)
What is the area, in mm², of a 20 mm diameter hole, to the nearest whole number? (π = 3.142)
What is the name of the average found by adding a set of values and dividing by how many values there are?
A cylinder pressure falls from 150 bar to 90 bar during a shift. What percentage of the starting pressure has been used?
A size is given as 75 ± 0.5 mm. What is the largest acceptable size, in mm?
A brace rises 700 mm over a level run of 1200 mm. To the nearest degree, what angle does it make with the level? (tan 30° = 0.577, tan 31° = 0.601)
A plasma cutter cuts at 750 mm/min. How many minutes does it take to cut 6 m of plate? (Ignore set-up time.)
Electrodes cost J$950 per kg. A job uses 7.5 kg. What is the cost of the electrodes, in J$?
A drawing is at a scale of 1:5. A part is 340 mm long. How long is it on the drawing, in mm?
What is the area, in square metres, of a sheet 2.4 m × 1.2 m?

essays.stem: Heat input HI (kJ/mm) = (V × I × 60) ÷ (1000 × S). Explain how to rearrange this formula to find the travel speed S, then work out the travel speed needed for a heat input of 1.2 kJ/mm at 25 V and 180 A.
essays.modelAnswer: To rearrange a formula, do the same thing to both sides until the unknown is on its own. Here S is on the bottom of the fraction. First multiply both sides by (1000 × S), which gives HI × 1000 × S = V × I × 60. Then divide both sides by (HI × 1000), which leaves S = (V × I × 60) ÷ (1000 × HI). Now put in the values: S = (25 × 180 × 60) ÷ (1000 × 1.2). The top is 25 × 180 = 4 500, and 4 500 × 60 = 270 000. The bottom is 1000 × 1.2 = 1 200. So S = 270 000 ÷ 1 200 = 225 mm/min. To check, put 225 back into the first formula: 270 000 ÷ (1000 × 225) = 1.2 kJ/mm, which is right. It also makes sense: a slower speed than this would give more heat input, and a faster speed less.
markingPoints: Explains doing the same to both sides to get the unknown alone
Correct rearranged formula S = (V × I × 60) ÷ (1000 × HI)
Substitutes the values correctly, showing working
Correct answer: 225 mm/min, with units
Checks the answer by putting it back, or by sense

essays.stem: A diagonal brace is to be fitted in a rectangular frame that measures 2.0 m wide and 1.5 m high between centre lines. Work out the brace length and the angle it makes with the bottom rail, and explain how you would check the result. (tan 36.87° = 0.75)
essays.modelAnswer: The brace is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle with a base of 2.0 m and a height of 1.5 m. By Pythagoras, the length is the square root of (2.0² + 1.5²) = the square root of (4.0 + 2.25) = the square root of 6.25 = 2.5 m between centre lines. For the angle with the bottom rail, tan of the angle = opposite ÷ adjacent = 1.5 ÷ 2.0 = 0.75, so the angle is 36.87°, about 37°. The angle at the top, with the side post, is 90° − 36.87° = 53.13°. The ends of the brace would be cut at these angles, and the length on the cut list must allow for the size of the members, because the 2.5 m is centre line to centre line. To check, I would note that the sides are in the ratio 3 : 4 : 5 (1.5 : 2.0 : 2.5), so the answer is sensible. On the job, I would check that the frame is square by measuring both diagonals before fitting the brace, then offer up the brace and check the fit before welding.
markingPoints: Uses Pythagoras correctly
Brace length 2.5 m between centre lines
Uses tan = opposite ÷ adjacent = 0.75, angle about 36.9° (other angle 53.1°)
Notes the cut length must allow for member sizes and end angles
Checks: 3-4-5 ratio, diagonals equal, trial fit before welding

essays.stem: A job has 24 m of 6 mm fillet weld (equal legs). Work out the volume and mass of weld metal, allowing 10% extra because welds are usually a little oversize, and the mass of electrodes to order if 60% of the electrode mass becomes weld metal. (Weld metal is 7.85 g/cm³.)
essays.modelAnswer: The cross-section of a fillet weld with equal legs is a right-angled triangle, so its area is ½ × 6 × 6 = 18 mm². Adding 10% for oversize gives 18 × 1.1 = 19.8 mm². The length is 24 m, which is 24 000 mm. The volume is area × length = 19.8 × 24 000 = 475 200 mm³. Since 1 cm³ is 1 000 mm³, this is 475.2 cm³. The mass is 475.2 × 7.85 = about 3 730 g, or 3.73 kg. Only about 60% of an electrode's mass ends up in the weld, because of the stub ends, spatter and the flux coating, so the electrodes needed are 3.73 ÷ 0.6 = about 6.2 kg. I would round this up and order about 6.5 kg, or the next full packet. A quick check: 18 mm² over 24 m is a little under half a litre, and steel weighs about 7.85 kg per litre, so about 3.7 kg is sensible.
markingPoints: Cross-section 18 mm², and 19.8 mm² with 10% added
Volume 475 200 mm³ = 475.2 cm³, with the unit change shown
Mass about 3.73 kg
Electrodes 3.73 ÷ 0.6 = about 6.2 kg, rounded up for ordering
Gives a reason for the 60% and checks the answer is sensible

essays.stem: Work out the materials price for a gate: steel J$38 500, electrodes and gas J$6 200, paint J$9 800. Add 10% for waste on the steel only, then a 20% mark-up on the total materials. Explain each step and say where GCT is added.
essays.modelAnswer: First the waste allowance is added to the steel only, because offcuts and saw cuts waste steel but the other items are bought as needed. 10% of J$38 500 is J$3 850, so the steel is J$38 500 + J$3 850 = J$42 350. Next, add up all the materials: J$42 350 + J$6 200 + J$9 800 = J$58 350. Then add the 20% mark-up, which covers handling, storage and some profit: 20% of J$58 350 is J$11 670, so the materials price is J$58 350 + J$11 670 = J$70 020. A quick check is J$58 350 × 1.2 = J$70 020. This is the price before tax. GCT is worked out at the current rate on the final price of the job (materials plus labour and any other charges), and shown on its own line on the quotation so the customer can see the price before and after tax. I would write down each figure and its source so that someone else can check the working.
markingPoints: Waste added to the steel only: J$42 350
Total materials J$58 350
Mark-up J$11 670, giving J$70 020
Explains each step (why waste on steel, what the mark-up covers) and checks
GCT added at the current rate on the final price and shown separately

essays.stem: A cylindrical water tank, 1.2 m in diameter and 1.8 m high with a flat top and bottom, is to be painted inside and outside. Work out the area to be painted and the paint needed for two coats, if the paint covers 10 m² per litre per coat. (π = 3.142)
essays.modelAnswer: The curved side is a rectangle when opened out: its length is the circumference, π × 1.2 = 3.770 m, and its height is 1.8 m, so the side area is 3.770 × 1.8 = about 6.79 m². The top and bottom are circles of radius 0.6 m. Each one is π × 0.6 × 0.6 = 1.131 m², so the two ends are 2.26 m². One surface of the tank is 6.79 + 2.26 = 9.05 m². Inside and outside doubles this to about 18.1 m². Two coats double it again, to 36.2 m² of painting. At 10 m² per litre, the paint needed is 36.2 ÷ 10 = 3.62 litres. Paint is sold in set sizes, and some is lost, so I would buy 4 litres. I would also check that the paint for the inside is safe for drinking water if the tank will hold it, and follow the maker's instructions for coverage and drying times between coats.
markingPoints: Curved side area about 6.79 m² (circumference × height)
Two ends about 2.26 m²
Total for one surface 9.05 m², doubled for inside and out (about 18.1 m²)
Two coats 36.2 m²; paint 3.62 L, rounded up to a sensible purchase
Mentions the maker's coverage figures or suitable paint for a water tank

essays.stem: Ten parts from a batch measure 249.6, 250.2, 250.4, 249.8, 250.0, 250.6, 249.4, 250.1, 249.9 and 250.0 mm. The drawing says 250 ± 0.5 mm. Work out the mean and the range, say which parts are out of tolerance, and explain what you would report.
essays.modelAnswer: The total of the ten sizes is 2 500.0 mm, so the mean is 2 500.0 ÷ 10 = 250.0 mm. The largest size is 250.6 mm and the smallest is 249.4 mm, so the range is 250.6 − 249.4 = 1.2 mm. The tolerance of ± 0.5 mm gives limits of 249.5 mm and 250.5 mm. The part at 250.6 mm is 0.1 mm too big, and the part at 249.4 mm is 0.1 mm too small, so 2 of the 10 parts, or 20%, are out of tolerance. The mean is right on size, but the range of 1.2 mm is wider than the 1.0 mm the tolerance allows, so the process is not steady enough. I would mark and set aside the two faulty parts, check the rest of the batch, and report the results in a table, with the mean, range and number rejected. I would suggest checking the cause, such as a loose stop on the saw or the way the parts are measured.
markingPoints: Mean 250.0 mm, with working
Range 1.2 mm
Limits 249.5 and 250.5 mm; the parts at 250.6 and 249.4 mm are out (20%)
Explains that the spread is wider than the tolerance band
Report: faulty parts set aside, batch checked, table of results, cause investigated

essays.stem: An imported procedure gives: preheat 200 °F, gas flow 25 cubic feet per hour, plate ½ inch, and gas pressure 30 psi. Convert each to metric, showing your working, and explain why care is needed. (1 ft³ = 28.3 L, 1 inch = 25.4 mm, 1 psi = 6.9 kPa)
essays.modelAnswer: Temperature: °C = (°F − 32) × 5 ÷ 9 = (200 − 32) × 5 ÷ 9 = 168 × 5 ÷ 9 = about 93 °C. Gas flow: 25 ft³ an hour × 28.3 L = about 708 L an hour, and dividing by 60 gives about 11.8 L/min, which matches the litres per minute marked on our flowmeters. Plate: ½ inch × 25.4 = 12.7 mm, so the nearest metric plate is 12 mm, and I would check with the supervisor whether 12 mm is allowed, because it is thinner. Pressure: 30 psi × 6.9 = about 207 kPa, or about 2.1 bar. Care is needed because a wrong conversion could give a wrong preheat or gas setting, or the wrong plate, which could make the weld fail. Each figure must be written with its unit, the conversion figure used should be checked, and the answer should be checked for sense, for example that 93 °C is a reasonable preheat. Any change, such as using 12 mm plate, needs approval.
markingPoints: Preheat about 93 °C, with working
Gas flow about 708 L/h or about 11.8 L/min
Plate 12.7 mm; notes the nearest metric size needs approval
Pressure about 207 kPa (about 2.1 bar)
Explains why care is needed: units shown, figures checked, answers checked for sense

essays.stem: Explain the ways you would check a calculation before it is used on the job, using a mass or a brace-length calculation as an example.
essays.modelAnswer: First check that the right formula and the right figures have been used, and that all the units are the same, for example all in metres or all in millimetres, before working it out. Then make a rough estimate. For the mass of a plate 2 m × 1 m × 10 mm, the volume is 0.02 m³, and steel is about 8 000 kg/m³, so it should be about 160 kg; the exact answer of 157 kg is close, but 1 570 kg would show a slip. Next, work the sum backwards, for example dividing the mass by the density to get the volume back. For a brace, check that the answer is longer than either side of the triangle but shorter than the two sides added together. Use a second method if there is one, such as a scale drawing. Write down the working step by step, so that another person can check it, and ask a team member to check important figures. Finally, check on the job, such as measuring both diagonals before cutting the brace.
markingPoints: Checks the formula, the figures and that the units match
Makes a rough estimate and compares (with a worked example)
Works backwards or uses a second method
Checks the answer makes sense (for example brace longer than each side)
Writes the working down, has it checked by another person, and checks on the job

essays.stem: A job needs 45 m of oxy-fuel cutting on 20 mm plate. The cutting speed is 400 mm/min and oxygen is used at 50 L/min. Work out the cutting time and the oxygen needed, allowing 20% extra for starts and waste, and say whether one cylinder holding about 6 800 L is enough.
essays.modelAnswer: First change the length to millimetres: 45 m = 45 000 mm. The cutting time is length ÷ speed = 45 000 ÷ 400 = 112.5 minutes, which is about 1 hour 53 minutes of cutting. The oxygen used while cutting is 112.5 × 50 = 5 625 litres. Adding 20% for preheating at starts, piercing and waste gives 5 625 × 1.2 = 6 750 litres. One cylinder holds about 6 800 litres, so on paper it is just enough, with only about 50 litres to spare. That is far too close: a cylinder cannot be emptied fully, the speed may be slower than planned, and some cuts may need to be redone. So I would plan to have a second full cylinder ready before starting, or order it at the same time. I would also plan breaks, because nearly two hours of cutting is a long time for one person, and record the actual gas used so that the next estimate is better.
markingPoints: Changes the units: 45 000 mm
Cutting time 112.5 minutes
Oxygen 5 625 L, and 6 750 L with 20% added
Judges that one cylinder is too close and plans a second cylinder, with reasons
Other sensible points: breaks, recording actual use

essays.stem: Describe how calculations for a job should be set out and recorded so that another person can check them. Include units, rounding and the use of a calculator.
essays.modelAnswer: Each calculation should start with a heading that says what is being worked out and for which job, drawing and part. Write down the information used, such as the sizes from the drawing and figures like the density of steel, with their sources. Write the formula in words or symbols, then the same formula with the numbers put in, then the answer. Keep one line for each step, so that a checker can follow it and find any mistake. Write the unit with every number, and change all the sizes to the same unit before starting. On a calculator, enter the sum carefully, use brackets where needed, and write down the full result before rounding. Round only at the end, to a sensible accuracy, such as the nearest 1 mm for a cut length or to one decimal place for a mass. Make a rough estimate to check the answer. Finally, sign and date the sheet, have a team member check and sign it, and file it with the job records.
markingPoints: Heading, job and part, and the data used with its source
Formula, then the numbers put in, then the answer, one step per line
Units with every number and all in the same unit
Careful calculator use; rounds only at the end to a sensible accuracy; rough check
Signed, dated, checked by another person and filed

practical1.title: Measure a fabricated item and calculate its mass, weld metal, paint and materials cost
practical1.brief: The assessor chooses a fabricated item at the Centre, such as a steel workbench, a gate or a stand, that can be safely measured and weighed. As a team, measure every part and make a dimensioned sketch and a parts list. Share out the calculations so that each member does at least one and another member checks it: (1) the length of each section and the total length of each size; (2) the mass of each part and of the whole item, using the section tables (kg/m) and 7850 kg/m³ for plate; (3) the total length of weld and an estimate of the weld metal and electrodes used; (4) the area to be painted and the paint needed for two coats at the coverage on the tin; and (5) the materials cost with a waste allowance, using the prices the assessor gives, with GCT at the rate the assessor gives. Then weigh the item with the Centre's scale or load cell, under the assessor's supervision, and work out the percentage difference between the calculated and the measured mass. Present the results on a calculation sheet. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and sheets to the group's practical.
materials: A fabricated item chosen by the assessor
Tape measures, steel rules, vernier calipers and a fillet weld gauge
Section mass tables and the price list from the assessor
The Centre's platform scale or a load cell with a suitable lifting aid
Calculation sheets, sketch paper, pens and calculators
Gloves and safety boots for each member
photos: Members measuring the item, with the tape or caliper visible
The dimensioned sketch and parts list
The calculation sheet for each member, showing the working and the checker's initials
The item on the scale, with the reading visible
The finished summary sheet: mass, weld, paint and cost, with the percentage difference
checklist: Measured accurately and recorded sizes with units
Did their calculation with the correct formula and working shown
Checked another member's calculation and corrected any errors
Took part in weighing the item safely
Worked out the percentage difference and gave a sensible reason for it
Presented the results clearly on the summary sheet
safety: Wear gloves and safety boots when handling the item
Lift the item onto the scale only with a lifting aid or a team lift, as the assessor directs
Check the scale or load cell is rated for the load before use
Keep walkways clear of tapes and sketch boards
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: Set out, cut and check a braced frame using trigonometry
practical2.brief: The assessor gives the team the outside sizes of a rectangular frame (for example 1200 mm × 900 mm) in square tube, with one diagonal brace and two corner gussets. As a team, work out on a calculation sheet: the cut length of each rail and post, allowing for the joint type; the length of the brace between the inside faces and its end cut angles, using Pythagoras and tan; the size and area of each gusset; and the length the frame diagonals should measure. Each member works out at least one part and another member checks it. Then mark out and cut the parts, lay them out on the welding table, and tack the frame. Check both diagonals and the brace fit against the calculation before welding. After welding, measure the frame and brace, compare them with the calculated sizes, and work out the error for each. Write down the likely causes of any differences. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and sheets to the group's practical.
materials: Square tube (for example 40 × 40 × 3 mm) and flat plate for the gussets
Cut-off saw or bandsaw, angle grinder, and a welding set (MIG or MMAW)
Tape, steel rule, combination square, protractor and scriber
Calculation sheet, calculators and a table of sine, cosine and tangent values (or calculators with these keys)
photos: The calculation sheet with the brace length and angles worked out and checked
The parts marked out, with the angles set on a protractor
The cut parts laid out on the table against the calculation
The tacked frame with both diagonals being measured
The welded frame with the brace in place
The results table comparing calculated and measured sizes
checklist: Worked out their part correctly, with working shown
Marked out and cut their part to the calculated size and angle
Measured the diagonals and corrected the frame before welding
Measured the finished frame accurately and recorded the results
Worked out the error correctly and gave sensible reasons for differences
safety: Wear full PPE for cutting, grinding and welding, with eye protection when grinding
Clamp work before cutting; keep hands clear of saw blades
Weld only in a booth or behind screens; warn others before striking an arc
Treat all cut and welded parts as hot: use tongs and mark hot work
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
